title: Acidic, Basic and Neutral Salts
short: Ions from weak acids or weak bases react with water and shift the pH.
trouble: Students think every salt solution is neutral because salts come from neutralization.

blocks.html: A salt is made of ions, and some ions are weak acids or weak bases. Using Ka × Kb = Kw and the weak-base method, you can predict and compute the pH of a salt solution.

Ions from strong acids and strong bases ($\mathrm{Cl^-}$, $\mathrm{NO_3^-}$, $\mathrm{Na^+}$, $\mathrm{K^+}$) do not change the pH. The conjugate base of a weak acid ($\mathrm{F^-}$, $\mathrm{CH_3COO^-}$, $\mathrm{CN^-}$) makes the solution basic. The conjugate acid of a weak base ($\mathrm{NH_4^+}$) makes it acidic, and so do small, highly charged metal ions such as $\mathrm{Al^{3+}}$ and $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}$.

$\mathrm{Cl^-}$ is the conjugate base of HCl, a strong acid, so its $K_b$ is essentially zero: it does not take protons from water. $\mathrm{CH_3COO^-}$ is the conjugate base of a weak acid, so its $K_b = K_w/K_a$ is small but real, and it makes a little $\mathrm{OH^-}$. A metal ion such as $\mathrm{Al^{3+}}$ is surrounded by water molecules; its strong positive charge pulls on their O–H bonds, and one of those waters can release a proton: $$\mathrm{[Al(H_2O)_6]^{3+}} + \mathrm{H_2O} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{[Al(H_2O)_5(OH)]^{2+}} + \mathrm{H_3O^+}$$

blocks.name: ch-phscale
blocks.cap: 0.10 M sodium acetate sits at pH 8.87: basic, though it came from a neutralization.

blocks.title: A basic salt
blocks.q: Find the pH of $0.10\ \text{M}$ $\mathrm{NaCH_3COO}$ ($K_a$ of acetic acid $= 1.8 \times 10^{-5}$).
steps: $\mathrm{Na^+}$ is a spectator. Acetate is a weak base with $K_b = \dfrac{1.0 \times 10^{-14}}{1.8 \times 10^{-5}} = 5.6 \times 10^{-10}$.

blocks.title: An acidic salt
steps: $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ is a spectator. $\mathrm{NH_4^+}$ is a weak acid: $K_a = \dfrac{1.0 \times 10^{-14}}{1.8 \times 10^{-5}} = 5.6 \times 10^{-10}$.

blocks.html: For a salt whose cation and anion both react, compare the two constants: the ion with the larger $K$ wins. In $\mathrm{NH_4CN}$, cyanide's $K_b$ is far larger than ammonium's $K_a$, so the solution is basic.

Thinking every salt solution is neutral because salts come from neutralization. Neutralizing a weak acid with a strong base leaves the weak acid's conjugate base, which reacts with water. Check: ask for each ion, "is it the partner of a weak acid or base?"
